traditions.name: Reformed
traditions.selfDescription: Reformed Christians confess that salvation is God's gracious work from first to last: the Father chose a people in Christ, the Son accomplished their redemption, and the Spirit unites them to Christ through the Word and the sacraments. We read the whole Bible as the story of one covenant of grace, summarize its teaching in confessions such as the Westminster Standards and the Three Forms of Unity, and seek to live all of life before the face of God, for his glory.
americanBodies: Christian Reformed Church in North America (CRCNA)
United Reformed Churches in North America (URCNA)
Reformed Baptist churches holding the 1689 London Baptist Confession
Westminster Theological Seminary; Reformed Theological Seminary; Covenant Theological Seminary
traditions.internalDiversity: Presbyterians (Westminster Standards) and Continental Reformed churches (Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort) baptize infants, while Reformed Baptists hold the 1689 London Baptist Confession and baptize believers only. There are further divisions over the millennium (mostly amillennial or postmillennial, some premillennial), over continuationism, over worship practice (exclusive psalmody versus hymns), and between confessional churches and the broader 'Calvinist' evangelical movement that shares Reformed soteriology without the confessions.

fairnessNotes: 'TULIP' as the first line of the framework: the acrostic is a much later English-language teaching device, not the wording of the Canons of Dort. Reformed historians (e.g. Richard Muller) warn it distorts Dort, and most Reformed writers say 'definite atonement' or 'particular redemption' rather than 'limited atonement'. Let the prompt cite Dort's five main points in its own terms.

'The absolute sovereignty of God as the controlling principle of all theology' restates the old 'central dogma' thesis that Reformed historians reject. Adherents would say the controlling principle is God's self-revelation in Scripture: the triune God of the covenant, with sovereignty as one attribute among his perfections.

The prompt names only the Westminster Confession. Continental Reformed churches (CRCNA, URCNA) confess the Three Forms of Unity (Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort), and Reformed Baptists confess the 1689 London Baptist Confession.

Key voices mix confessional Reformed theologians with Calvinistic Baptists whose views the framework says they hold. Spurgeon, Piper and Grudem are Baptists (Piper and Grudem are also premillennial and open to continuing spiritual gifts). They reject infant baptism and Westminster-style covenant theology, so they cannot speak for the 'Westminster Confession as a confessional standard'. Either drop them or describe the voice as 'Reformed and Calvinistic Baptist'.

Martyn Lloyd-Jones is respected but unusual: a Welsh-born nonconformist preacher (Westminster Chapel, London) who taught a distinct post-conversion 'sealing' or baptism of the Spirit that most confessional Reformed theologians reject.

traditions.name: Wesleyan / Arminian
traditions.selfDescription: We believe God truly loves every person and that Christ died for all. By prevenient grace the Holy Spirit goes before every human heart and frees the will to respond to the gospel, so salvation is wholly by grace through faith, yet never forced. Wesleyans add that grace aims at holiness of heart and life: the Spirit can so fill a believer with love for God and neighbor that love becomes the ruling motive of life.
americanBodies: The United Methodist Church (doctrinal standards; also counted as mainline)
National Association of Free Will Baptists (Reformed Arminian)
traditions.internalDiversity: Wesleyan-Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan, Free Methodist, Salvation Army) teach entire sanctification as a second work of grace; Methodists broadly speak of 'going on to perfection'; Reformed Arminians (Free Will Baptists) reject entire sanctification, hold a penal-satisfaction view of the atonement, and teach that true apostasy happens only through unbelief. Arminians differ on whether election is individual and based on foreseen faith or corporate 'in Christ', and many Baptists and Pentecostals hold Arminian views without the Wesleyan label.

fairnessNotes: The description's headline 'Free Will' invites the semi-Pelagian caricature Arminians reject. Arminius and Wesley both taught total depravity; the will is 'freed' by prevenient grace, not naturally free. Better: 'Prevenient Grace · Resistible Grace · Christ Died for All'.

The label 'Arminian / Wesleyan' plus 'Wesley's doctrine of entire sanctification' in the framework speaks only for Wesleyans. Reformed Arminians (Free Will Baptists: Picirilli, Forlines, Pinson) and many Baptist and Pentecostal Arminians reject entire sanctification. Present it as the Wesleyan-Holiness emphasis, not the whole tradition's.

'Conditional election: God foreknows who will believe and elects accordingly' is the classic view but not the only one; some Arminians teach corporate election in Christ (e.g. Robert Shank, Elect in the Son).

'The possibility of apostasy (falling from grace)' merges two views: Wesleyans generally hold that backsliders can be restored; Reformed Arminians teach that apostasy happens only through unbelief and cannot be undone (the FWB Treatise ch. XIII speaks of believers being 'in danger of falling').
Key voices omit the Reformed Arminian and Holiness streams (e.g. Pinson, H. Orton Wiley), so the voice leans Methodist.

traditions.name: Fundamentalist
traditions.selfDescription: Fundamentalists are Bible-believing Christians who hold that the fundamentals of the faith must be believed and defended, not merely assumed: the verbally inspired, inerrant Word of God, the virgin birth and deity of Christ, his substitutionary blood atonement, his bodily resurrection and his literal return. Because Scripture commands God's people to keep the faith pure, we practice biblical separation from apostasy and from ministries that cooperate with it, while giving ourselves to holy living, soul-winning and strong local churches.
americanBodies: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches (GARBC)
keyVoices: Charles H. Spurgeon (claimed as a forerunner for the Downgrade Controversy)
traditions.internalDiversity: Self-described 'historic' fundamentalists (Central Seminary, Detroit Seminary, FBFI, BJU) differ from much of the independent Baptist world over King James Only convictions, revivalist methods and authoritarian pastoral styles, which Central Seminary calls 'hyper-fundamentalism'. They also differ on how far separation extends (secondary separation from evangelicals who cooperate with non-evangelicals), and a minority are Calvinist or non-dispensational. The movement also had Presbyterian fundamentalists (Bible Presbyterian Church).

fairnessNotes: Key voices: J. Frank Norris shot and killed a man in his church office in 1926 (he was acquitted). Self-described historic fundamentalists treat him as a cautionary figure, not a model.

Key voices: Jerry Falwell Sr.'s Moral Majority cooperation was opposed by separatist fundamentalists such as Bob Jones Jr. Carl McIntire was a Presbyterian separatist, and Clarence Larkin was a dispensational chart illustrator. None of the three speaks well for the movement's theology as such. Better: Torrey, Dixon, Riley, John R. Rice, Ernest Pickering, Kevin Bauder.

'Dispensational premillennialism' is listed as a defining tenet. It is dominant (GARBC and IFCA are premillennial), but the original fundamentalist coalition included non-dispensationalists (e.g. Presbyterian fundamentalists), and fundamentalists define themselves by the fundamentals plus separation, not by eschatology.

'A high view of the local church and pastoral authority' reads as a nod to authoritarian independent-Baptist culture, which historic fundamentalists explicitly oppose (Central Seminary rejects 'hyper-fundamentalism'). Adherents would say 'local church autonomy' and 'biblical separation'.

'Suspicion of ecumenism, cultural compromise' frames separation as a mood. Adherents frame it as obedience to a biblical command (FBFI's constitution speaks of 'the mandate of biblical separation'). 'Neo-evangelical' is their own term, so it can stay.
The 'KJV or NKJV' instruction is right for many independent Baptists, but BJU, Central and Detroit Seminary are not King James Only; avoid making KJV-onlyism part of the voice.

traditions.name: Evangelical
traditions.selfDescription: Evangelicals are gospel people: we believe the Bible is God's inspired and fully trustworthy Word, that Jesus Christ died in our place and rose bodily from the dead, and that every person needs to be born again through personal faith in him. That gospel shapes everything else: evangelism and world missions, Bible-centered preaching, prayer and holy living, and faithful engagement with culture, across many denominations and in nondenominational churches.
americanBodies: Wheaton College; Trinity Evangelical Divinity School
traditions.internalDiversity: Evangelicals are divided between Calvinists and non-Calvinists (a live debate inside the SBC), between complementarians and egalitarians on women's roles, between cessationists and continuationists, over baptism (believers-only versus infant baptism in evangelical Presbyterian and Anglican churches), and over eschatology. Some hold strict inerrancy in the Chicago Statement sense; others prefer 'infallible' or 'trustworthy' language.

fairnessNotes: 'Tim Keller (in his more conservative moments)' is a dig, not a description. Keller was a PCA minister bound to the Westminster Standards throughout his ministry; adherents would reject the implication that he was only intermittently conservative. (He died in 2023.)

'Biblical authority and inerrancy (Chicago Statement), but engaged with scholarship' implies inerrancy and scholarship pull against each other. Evangelicals see inerrancy as a scholarly position (ETS was founded as a scholarly society on that basis). Drop 'but'.

Francis Chan has since moved to a house-church model and has spoken publicly about his changing views of the Lord's Supper, so he is a debated example of the evangelical center. John Stott, J. I. Packer or D. A. Carson are safer.

The tradition is described as 'Southern Baptist, non-denominational' but the framework silently assumes Calvinist-leaning voices (Mohler, Keller, Platt). Many Southern Baptists and nondenominational evangelicals are not Calvinists, so the voice should not default to Reformed soteriology.

traditions.name: Progressive Evangelical
traditions.selfDescription: We are evangelicals who believe the gospel of Jesus is good news for the whole person and the whole world: personal conversion and discipleship belong together with justice for the poor, racial reconciliation, the equal partnership of women and men, and care for creation. We take the words and way of Jesus, especially the Sermon on the Mount, as the center of Christian ethics, and we call the church to repent wherever it has been captured by wealth, racism or partisan politics.
americanBodies: Christians for Social Action (formerly Evangelicals for Social Action)
traditions.internalDiversity: The older evangelical left (Sider, Perkins, the 1973 Chicago Declaration) generally held traditional sexual ethics and often a consistent pro-life ethic, while many younger voices affirm same-sex marriage. Campolo did so in 2015; Sider did not. Some prefer 'Red Letter Christian' or 'post-evangelical' to 'evangelical' at all, and the movement ranges from Anabaptist-leaning peace churches to mainline-adjacent progressives.

fairnessNotes: Several key voices did not, or no longer, identify with this tradition. N. T. Wright is a Church of England bishop with traditional views on sexuality who does not use the label. Eugene Peterson was a PC(USA) (mainline) pastor. Richard Foster is a Quaker spiritual-formation writer. Rachel Held Evans publicly left evangelicalism for the Episcopal Church before her death in 2019. Brian McLaren and Rob Bell have moved beyond evangelical identity. Scot McKnight is debatable. Better: Sider, Perkins, Campolo, Wallis, Claiborne, Harper, Rah.

'Engagement with postmodern culture and interfaith dialogue' and 'generous orthodoxy' describe the 2000s emerging church (McLaren's 2004 book title, borrowed from Hans Frei), not the evangelical-left lineage of the 1973 Chicago Declaration, ESA/CSA, Sojourners and CCDA, which stresses evangelism plus justice ('the whole gospel').

'Commitment to biblical authority alongside historical-critical scholarship' is not a defining mark: the Chicago Declaration signers and Sider held a high, traditional view of Scripture. Adherents would say they take the words of Jesus with full seriousness, not that they adopt historical criticism.

'The Kingdom of God as present social reality, not just future hope' is fair, but adherents insist on both personal conversion and social transformation; the prompt never mentions evangelism or personal faith, which makes the voice sound mainline rather than evangelical.

The name itself is contested: Campolo and Claiborne coined 'Red Letter Christians' partly because 'evangelical' had become politically loaded. Note that some in this stream reject both 'progressive' and 'evangelical'.

traditions.name: Mainline Protestant
traditions.selfDescription: Mainline Protestants belong to the historic denominations that shaped American public life, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran, United Church of Christ and others, and we confess the faith of the ancient creeds within our own Reformed, Wesleyan, Anglican or Lutheran heritage. We read Scripture as the living witness to God's Word made flesh in Jesus Christ, interpreted in community with tradition, reason and the best of scholarship. We believe God's grace calls the church to welcome all people and to work for justice and peace, because, as the UCC puts it, 'God is still speaking.'
americanBodies: National Council of the Churches of Christ in the USA
traditions.internalDiversity: 'Mainline' names a family of denominations, not one theology: each keeps its own confessional heritage (PC(USA)'s Book of Confessions, Methodist Articles of Religion and Wesley's sermons, the Episcopal Book of Common Prayer, the ELCA's Lutheran confessions), and their sacramental theology differs accordingly. Each also contains liberal, moderate and evangelical wings, though many theological conservatives have left (for example the UMC disaffiliations of 2019-2023, when roughly a quarter of US congregations left).

fairnessNotes: The grouping blurs real sacramental and confessional differences. The ELCA is Lutheran in sacramental theology: it confesses Christ's real presence in the Lord's Supper and baptismal regeneration and holds the Augsburg Confession as a constitutional standard. The Episcopal Church is Anglican (Book of Common Prayer, bishops in historic succession). PC(USA) is Reformed (its Book of Confessions includes Westminster and Heidelberg). The UMC is Wesleyan. On sacraments topics these churches will not answer alike, even though they are in full communion with one another (ELCA with PC(USA) and UCC through the 1997 Formula of Agreement, with TEC through Called to Common Mission, with the UMC since 2009).

'Christianity is fundamentally about social transformation' and 'this-worldly justice over otherworldly salvation' are critics' framings. Mainline confessions still speak of forgiveness of sins and eternal life (e.g. the UCC Statement of Faith, the BCP Catechism), and adherents would say justice flows from grace rather than replacing salvation.

Bultmann was a German Lutheran who never belonged to an American church. Spong is treated by many in his own Episcopal Church as an outlier, since he rejected theism in his 'Twelve Points'. Neither is representative of mainline teaching. Missing figures adherents would name: the Niebuhrs, Fosdick, Brueggemann, Barbara Brown Taylor.

'United Methodist (progressive wing)' is outdated: after about a quarter of US congregations disaffiliated (2019-2023), the 2024 General Conference removed the denomination's restrictions on LGBTQ clergy and weddings, so this is now the UMC's official position, not a wing's.

'Liberal' was a self-chosen label for Fosdick's generation, but most mainline members today would say 'mainline' or 'progressive'. Each denomination also has moderate and evangelical members, so the prompt should speak for mainline theology, not for every mainline Christian.

'Process theology, liberation theology, and feminist theology' are influential in mainline seminaries, but none is the official doctrine of any of these denominations; present them as influences, not tenets.

traditions.name: Pentecostal / Charismatic
traditions.selfDescription: Pentecostals and charismatics believe the same Holy Spirit who came on the day of Pentecost is poured out on believers today, empowering them to witness for Jesus with the gifts of the Spirit, including tongues, prophecy and healing. We proclaim Jesus as Savior, Healer, Baptizer in the Holy Spirit and soon-coming King, and we expect to meet God's presence in worship and prayer. Classical Pentecostals teach that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after salvation, with speaking in other tongues as its initial physical evidence.
americanBodies: Charismatic renewal in Catholic and mainline churches
Oral Roberts University; Regent University; Lee University; Evangel University
traditions.internalDiversity: Classical Pentecostals (AG, Church of God, IPHC) teach subsequence and initial evidence. Holiness Pentecostals (Church of God, IPHC, COGIC) add sanctification as a definite work of grace. Charismatics in older denominations and 'Third Wave' churches (Vineyard) usually reject initial evidence and see Spirit baptism as part of conversion or as repeated fillings. Oneness Pentecostals (e.g. the United Pentecostal Church International) reject the Trinity and are not recognized as orthodox by Trinitarian Pentecostals. The movement is also divided over prosperity teaching and over modern-day apostles and prophets.

fairnessNotes: The framework states 'Baptism in the Holy Spirit as a distinct experience subsequent to conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues' as the shared view. That is the classical Pentecostal position (AG Truth 8; Church of God; IPHC), but charismatics in historic churches and the Third Wave or Vineyard stream it names usually reject both subsequence and initial evidence. Attribute it to classical Pentecostals.

'Divine healing is in the atonement; God desires physical healing for believers' is close to AG and IPHC wording ('provided for in the atonement'), but the second clause drifts toward Word of Faith. Pentecostal denominations distinguish themselves from that movement, so keep the confessional wording.
Charles Parham taught initial evidence first (1901), but his racism and personal scandal mean many Pentecostals today honor Seymour and Azusa Street, not Parham, as their founding figure.

Wayne Grudem is a Reformed Baptist continuationist who rejects a second-blessing Spirit baptism; he speaks for continuationism, not for Pentecostal or charismatic tradition. Bill Johnson (Bethel) is popular but contested within classical Pentecostalism (the AG has a position paper on 'modern-day apostles'), so he is a debatable choice as a representative.
Key voices omit Black Pentecostalism beyond Seymour; Charles H. Mason and COGIC, one of the largest Pentecostal bodies in the US, should be represented.

traditions.name: Word of Faith
traditions.selfDescription: Word of Faith believers are Spirit-filled Christians who take God's promises at face value: what Jesus purchased at the cross includes forgiveness, healing for the body and redemption from the curse of the law, and faith receives it by believing and speaking God's Word. Following teachers such as Kenneth E. Hagin, we emphasize the integrity of the Word, the believer's authority in Christ, and walking in God's blessing, spirit, soul and body, so that we can live in victory and be a blessing to others.
emphases: redeemed from the curse of the law
faith comes by hearing the Word
americanBodies: Kenneth Hagin Ministries, Rhema Bible Church and Rhema Bible Training College (Broken Arrow, OK)
Andrew Wommack Ministries and Charis Bible College
Creflo Dollar Ministries / World Changers Church International
traditions.internalDiversity: Hagin's Rhema stream emphasizes faith, healing and the believer's authority and later cautioned against prosperity excesses (Hagin's The Midas Touch, 2000), while other ministries put more weight on financial prosperity and seed-faith giving. Teachers differ on how far the believer's authority and 'confession' extend, on tithing (Creflo Dollar publicly revised his earlier tithing teaching in 2022), and on how they relate to classical Pentecostal denominations.

fairnessNotes: 'Believers are little gods' is not in any Word of Faith statement of faith (Rhema, ICFM, AWMI). It comes from isolated sermon remarks that critics publicized, notably Hank Hanegraaff's Christianity in Crisis (1993). Rhema's statement says 'Man is a created being' and confesses one God in three Persons. Presenting 'little gods' as a tenet puts words in the tradition's mouth; remove it, or at most note the 'believers share Christ's authority' theme in their own words.

'Health and wealth gospel' (in the framework) and 'Prosperity · Confession · Health & Wealth' (the description) are critics' labels. Adherents do use 'prosperity': ICFM's statement has 'Prosperity: Spirit, Soul and Body' and KCM has a prosperity topic. But they frame it as redemption from 'the curse of the law which is poverty, sickness and death' (ICFM), divine healing 'provided for in the atonement' (Rhema), and the believer's authority. Better description: 'Faith · Healing · The Believer's Authority'.

'Faith is a spiritual force that, when activated through positive confession, releases God's power' reads as mind-over-matter. Copeland does speak of 'the force of faith', but the Hagin stream frames faith as believing and speaking what God's Word says (Mark 11:23-24; Rom 10:10) and denies that it is positive thinking. Use their scriptural wording.
'Negative confession ... can block or forfeit God's blessings' is a real teaching, but stated alone it sounds like superstition; adherents tie it to Proverbs 18:21 and to faith versus unbelief.

Joel Osteen does not identify as Word of Faith and his preaching is mainly motivational, so including him is debatable. The list also omits Kenneth W. Hagin (who now leads Rhema), Frederick K. C. Price and Andrew Wommack. Hagin Sr.'s own critique of prosperity excesses (The Midas Touch, 2000) shows the tradition corrects itself and should be represented.

traditions.name: Dispensational
traditions.selfDescription: Dispensationalists read the Bible with a consistently normal, grammatical-historical hermeneutic and see God administering his one purpose through successive stewardships, or dispensations, all of them saving by grace through faith. Because God keeps his unconditional covenant promises, we believe national Israel still has a future in God's program distinct from the church, and we look for the imminent return of Christ for his church, followed by the tribulation and Christ's literal thousand-year reign on David's throne.
americanBodies: Friends of Israel Gospel Ministry; Ariel Ministries
traditions.internalDiversity: Classical dispensationalism (Darby, Scofield, Chafer) contrasted Israel's earthly destiny with the church's heavenly one. Revised or normative dispensationalism (Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost) kept the Israel-church distinction without that dualism. Progressive dispensationalism (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) sees the church as an inaugurated stage of the one Davidic kingdom. Most hold a pretribulational rapture, but adherents differ on how much of the New Covenant applies to the church now.

fairnessNotes: 'A sharp distinction between Israel (earthly promises) and the Church (heavenly calling)' is classical dispensationalism only. Revised dispensationalists (Ryrie, Walvoord) dropped the earthly/heavenly dualism, and progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) reject it. State the Israel-church distinction without the dualism, or label it classical.

'Literal interpretation of all biblical prophecy' invites the wooden-literalism caricature. Adherents say a 'normal', 'plain' or 'grammatical-historical' hermeneutic, consistently applied (Ryrie's sine qua non), which recognizes figures of speech.

Hal Lindsey (died 2024) and Tim LaHaye were popularizers. Scholarly dispensationalists distance themselves from prophecy speculation and would name Chafer, McClain, Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie, Saucy, Blaising and Bock.

'Dallas Theological Seminary as the institutional home of classical dispensationalism' is dated: DTS's own faculty includes progressive dispensationalists (Darrell Bock), and Moody Bible Institute and The Master's Seminary also teach premillennial positions that keep Israel distinct from the church.

The framework never says dispensationalists believe salvation has always been by grace through faith. Critics often claim dispensationalism teaches multiple ways of salvation, which adherents explicitly deny; the prompt should say so.

traditions.name: Open Theism (the open view of God)
traditions.selfDescription: Open theists believe the God revealed in Jesus is a God of love who created a world of genuine relationship, where creatures' choices and prayers really matter. God knows all of reality perfectly, including every possibility, but because God chose to create free agents, the future is partly settled and partly open. God is infinitely wise and resourceful, never caught off guard, and engages in real give-and-take with us, as Scripture portrays.
americanBodies: No denomination officially holds open theism; adherents are found mainly in Arminian, Wesleyan, Baptist, Anabaptist-leaning and Adventist settings
ReKnew (Greg Boyd) and Woodland Hills Church, St. Paul, MN
Center for Open and Relational Theology
traditions.internalDiversity: Open theists differ on why the future is open: some say God limits his own foreknowledge, while most say future free choices are not yet there to be known, so not knowing them is no limit on omniscience. They also differ on how close to stay to classical theism (evangelical open theists such as Boyd and Sanders versus 'open and relational' thinkers influenced by process thought, such as Oord) and on how to read the biblical texts about divine repentance.

fairnessNotes: The description 'God Learns' is the critics' headline. Open theists say God knows all of reality perfectly; future free choices are not yet reality to be known, so God's knowledge of them as possibilities is complete (Boyd: open theism is about the nature of the future, not a deficiency in God). Better: 'Open Future · Relational God · Responsive Providence'.

'God ... does not exhaustively foreknow future free choices' frames the view as a limit on omniscience. Most adherents state it positively: God exhaustively knows all that is knowable, including what might happen.

'Open theism is a development within evangelical Arminianism' is only partly true. Richard Rice, whose 1980 book The Openness of God named the view, is a Seventh-day Adventist; Boyd's ReKnew is Anabaptist-leaning; and 'open and relational' theologians such as Oord stand partly outside evangelicalism.

'Classical theism's notions ... reflect Greek philosophy more than Scripture' is their argument (Pinnock's critique of the 'biblical-classical synthesis') and is fair to include, but it should be presented as their claim, not as an assumed fact.
There are no confessions or denominational statements for open theism, so its sources are necessarily books and articles by its proponents. The prompt should not imply institutional backing it lacks.

traditions.name: Lutheran
traditions.selfDescription: Lutherans confess that sinners are justified by grace alone, through faith alone, on account of Christ alone, and that God delivers this gift through his Word and sacraments. In Baptism God gives new birth, and in the Lord's Supper Christ's true body and blood are given with the bread and wine for the forgiveness of sins. We distinguish Law from Gospel, teach a theology of the cross, and receive the Book of Concord, above all the Augsburg Confession, as a faithful exposition of Scripture.
americanBodies: Lutheran Congregations in Mission for Christ (LCMC)
Concordia Seminary (St. Louis); Concordia Theological Seminary (Fort Wayne)
traditions.internalDiversity: Confessional Lutherans (LCMS, WELS) subscribe to the whole Book of Concord because it agrees with Scripture, hold inerrancy, ordain only men and practice close(d) communion. The ELCA accepts the Augsburg Confession and the other confessions as true witnesses, ordains women and LGBTQ clergy, is in full communion with Reformed, Episcopal and Methodist churches, and signed the 1999 Joint Declaration on justification with the Catholic Church. The NALC and LCMC sit in between. Translations follow the split: LCMS uses the ESV, the ELCA the NRSV.

fairnessNotes: No current prompt. If added, do not fold Lutherans into 'Reformed' or generic 'evangelical': Lutherans reject the Reformed view of the Lord's Supper (Formula of Concord VII) and teach baptismal regeneration.
Do not describe the real presence as 'consubstantiation'. Lutherans generally reject the term and prefer the sacramental union, with Christ's body and blood 'in, with and under' the bread and wine.

Decide which Lutheran voice speaks. LCMS/WELS and ELCA answers differ on Scripture, ordination, sexuality and ecumenism, and the ELCA also sits inside 'mainline_liberal'. Either specify 'confessional Lutheran' or describe the split.

traditions.name: Catholic
traditions.selfDescription: Catholics believe Jesus Christ founded one Church on the apostles, whose successors, the bishops in communion with the Pope, hand on the Word of God through Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, faithfully interpreted by the Magisterium. Christ's grace comes to us above all through the seven sacraments, with the Eucharist, his real Body and Blood, as 'the source and summit of the Christian life', and God calls every person to holiness and eternal communion with the Holy Trinity.
americanBodies: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) and the Latin-rite dioceses
Eastern Catholic churches in the US (e.g. Ruthenian, Ukrainian, Maronite, Melkite)
The Catholic University of America; University of Notre Dame
EWTN; Word on Fire; Catholic Answers
traditions.internalDiversity: Catholics share one dogmatic framework, but in the US they differ sharply in emphasis: traditionalists drawn to the pre-1970 Latin Mass, 'JPII/Benedict' conservatives, and progressive Catholics focused on social teaching. They also differ on how to apply Catholic social teaching to politics and on the reception of recent papal teaching. Eastern Catholics share Catholic doctrine but follow Byzantine or other Eastern liturgies and spiritual traditions.

Catholic teaching is that justification is by grace (see Trent Session 6 and the 1999 Joint Declaration with Lutherans), that Mary is venerated rather than worshipped, and that Scripture and Tradition flow from one 'divine wellspring' (DV 9).
Cite the Catechism and council documents by paragraph number. Individual theologians or popular apologists should not be treated as magisterial.

traditions.name: Eastern Orthodox
traditions.selfDescription: The Orthodox Church understands itself as the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church, guarding unchanged the faith of the apostles, the Church Fathers and the seven Ecumenical Councils. Salvation is theosis: by grace, through the Holy Mysteries (the sacraments), prayer and ascetic struggle, human beings come to share in the life of the Holy Trinity. Theology is lived above all in the Divine Liturgy, where heaven and earth meet.
americanBodies: Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America
Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian and Russian (ROCOR) Orthodox dioceses
Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops of the United States of America
St Vladimir's Orthodox Theological Seminary; Holy Cross Greek Orthodox School of Theology; St Tikhon's Seminary
keyVoices: the Cappadocian Fathers (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa)
traditions.internalDiversity: Orthodox churches share one faith but are organized by jurisdiction (Greek, Russian, Antiochian, Serbian and others), which sometimes clash. The 2016 Holy and Great Council in Crete went ahead without Antioch, Russia, Bulgaria and Georgia, and jurisdictions differ on ecumenism, the calendar, and the reception of converts. The Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Syriac) are a separate communion that does not accept the Council of Chalcedon.

fairnessNotes: No current prompt. If added, do not present Orthodoxy as 'Catholicism without the Pope' or as merely 'Eastern' style. It rejects the filioque, papal supremacy and later Western developments such as purgatory as defined in the West, and it frames theology through theosis and the Liturgy rather than Western legal categories.
'Theosis' means participation in God's uncreated energies by grace, not becoming God by nature (the essence-energies distinction). Phrase it carefully.
Orthodox call the sacraments 'Holy Mysteries' and do not fix their number as dogmatically as Rome. The prompt should not impose a seven-sacrament checklist as Orthodox dogma without that nuance.
